entries.title: Trump Administration Delays Iowa Lead Detonation to Wednesday
entries.summary: The administration said it would be investigating the contractor that runs the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for how it handled the lead explosives.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is again delaying the planned detonation of lead explosives in Iowa, this time to Wednesday, after widespread outcry from communities furious that they were not sufficiently warned about the possibility of a toxic lead plume.

The White House is expected to investigate how dangerous lead azide explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant were allowed to deteriorate to the point that they needed to be detonated, as well as launch a probe into the contractor that manages the plant, a source familiar with the situation told The Washington Sun.

American Ordnance, the contractor responsible for managing the explosives at the plant, and its inspectors discovered the deterioration in the lead in March 2026, according to EPA permitting documents and Army communications reviewed by The Sun.

The White House, led by President Donald Trump’s new chief of staff Stephen Miller, convened a team of agency leaders alongside the Homeland Security Council and National Security Council over the past 48 hours to discuss why the explosives had to be detonated and how to mitigate potential risks to the public, the source said. Senior White House officials only became aware of the issue Thursday, even though the Army has been planning how to deal with the problem for about six months.

The source requested anonymity to describe details of the unfolding situation.

The Army had already delayed its planned detonation of 68 barrels of degrading lead azide to Monday from the Friday original schedule, warning that was the latest possible date before the risks of an uncontrolled explosion became too great.

Sunday night, the Army posted to X that the detonation would occur Wednesday “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.”

“The Army and our interagency partners have been working around the clock to safeguard all Americans in the region,” the Army said in the post. “Additional details on this situation will be forthcoming. The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority.”

The administration said in court filings that cold temperatures will dramatically increase the chances that the lead azide — which has been degrading for months — could spontaneously explode, sparking a public panic over a lead dust plume spreading in the air above the Middletown plant.

The Army insisted in court filings over the weekend that the explosion could not be delayed past Tuesday, at the latest, because of the risks. While a federal court temporarily blocked the EPA permit authorizing the explosion, Justice Department attorneys warned that the Army would proceed with the detonation plan regardless of the judge’s ruling because it deemed the situation to be an emergency that merited operating without a permit.

The Army also revealed in court filings that it previously considered and then abandoned a plan to neutralize the lead azide with chemicals, warning that it would be too dangerous for anyone to try opening the lids of the barrels holding the lead in order to do the chemical treatment.

“So this was truly a choice between controlled or uncontrolled detonation,” the source familiar with the situation said. Now the discussion has moved on to how the government can put “as many mitigation measures in place as possible to protect the public.”

Public anxiety about the dangers of a lead plume escalated over the weekend with news of the pending explosion. An Army official familiar with the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter, told The Sun that the “exposure for the unmitigated worst case scenario here would be roughly equivalent to living in Los Angeles or New York City for three days in 1985.” Leaded gasoline was still in use at that time, making ambient lead exposure relatively quite high compared to today.

No amount of lead is safe to ingest, according to public health experts. Lead is a toxin that is especially dangerous to children, who are more sensitive to brain and nerve system damage.

Iowa officials, including Gov. Kim Reynolds, said they were only made aware of the Army’s plans to detonate the explosive one week ago, when the Army published maps showing a possible lead dust plume stretching across southeastern Iowa and into Illinois.

The Army increased the risk of an uncontrolled explosion in preparation for the original detonation date by removing the heavy metal bunker doors protecting the lead azide. Now those doors cannot be replaced, and the explosive is more vulnerable to swings in cold temperatures, The Sun previously reported.

“Unfavorable winds could increase the dispersion of lead dust into the community,” according to a DOJ filing in court. “An uncontrolled deportation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast — harm that cannot be undone.”

Iowa environmental groups on Thursday sued the EPA — which permitted the detonation — in an effort to try to delay the scheduled explosion. The Army is not party to the suit.
